metadata.title: Why Individual Caution Does Not Add Up to Team Safety
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: five individually careful people using Claude on a team do not automatically add up to a careful team, because agents act on shared assets and the accountability gap sits at the boundary between people, not inside anyone's practice. Lands the carry-out that team safety lives in the fence around what's shared, not in individual carefulness.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (four fenced individuals plus one unfenced shared center, planted with no fence drawn around the center; returns with a new fence drawn around the shared center, labeled with the three rules)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes that if each person is careful, they're personally safe. But the real exposure isn't personal at all — it's shared. So the real question: does five careful people add up to one safe team?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Five careful people using Claude on a team. Does that make us safe?', hesitates on 'us', corrects to 'the team'

props.text:
Five careful people
using Claude on a team.
Does that make
us safe?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. Single-word trigger ('us') so buildActs()'s whitespace-token match fires (per the constitution/IVP/MPC redo lesson on multi-word triggers); replacement ('the team') may contain a space since it is only typed, never matched. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('us' -> 'the team') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Say four teammates each use Claude carefully, on their own account. One adds a connector to read the shared team Dropbox. It's added at the account level — not just for that person. All four teammates' agents can now read every file in Dropbox, including a client contract marked confidential. No one intended this. No one knew.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - four nodes each inside a small fence, one unfenced shared folder in the center; the confidential file appears inside it

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - four fenced individuals, one unfenced shared center
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four small nodes appear, each inside its own teal fence. A shared-folder icon appears in the center, no fence around it. An arrow from one fenced node connects a plug to the shared folder; a confidential-contract file inside it gets flagged terracotta. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: four people who are each careful with Claude should add up to a team that's careful too.

shot.new_visual_element: Four checkmarks arrow upward into one big TEAM SAFE checkmark

production_viz.label: The natural guess - individual care sums to team safety
production_viz.mechanic: Four small checkmarks appear in a row, one per teammate. Arrows converge upward from each into one large checkmark labeled 'TEAM SAFE'. Sell the aggregation as reasonable.

beats.narration_text: But nobody approved that connector for the whole team — only one person clicked add, for their own use. The account doesn't know the difference. The gap doesn't show up inside anyone's careful practice. It shows up at the boundary between people, in the shared space nobody owns.

shot.new_visual_element: The TEAM SAFE checkmark struck through; zoom into the boundary between the fenced nodes and the shared center, labeled NOBODY'S FENCE

production_viz.label: The break - the gap sits at the boundary, not inside any practice
production_viz.mechanic: The B02 'TEAM SAFE' checkmark is struck through with a terracotta line. The view zooms into the boundary between the four fenced nodes and the unfenced shared folder from B01; a label reads 'NOBODY'S FENCE' over that empty boundary strip.

beats.narration_text: The shared folder was never any one person's responsibility to fence. It belonged to all four accounts equally — which in practice meant it belonged to none of them.

shot.new_visual_element: The shared folder with four arrows pointing in from the fenced nodes, no owner, a dotted absent-fence outline

production_viz.label: Owned by all four accounts, which meant owned by none
production_viz.mechanic: The shared folder sits center with four thin arrows pointing in from each of the four fenced nodes, all equal weight. A dotted outline sketches where a fence would go, then fades — no one draws it.

beats.narration_text: That doesn't mean every shared thing needs a rule. One teammate quietly reading their own files under their own login isn't a team-level risk — the fence only needs to go up around what's actually shared.

shot.new_visual_element: One node reading its own private file, small and unfenced, no alarm, contrasted with the open shared node

production_viz.label: Not everything needs a fence - a private read isn't a team risk
production_viz.mechanic: One fenced node quietly opens its own private file inside its own fence — small icon, calm, no alarm color. Beside it, the shared folder from B01 sits open with no fence, visibly the different case.

beats.narration_text: Back to the four teammates: the fix was never asking anyone to be more careful — they already were. It's naming, before anyone connects anything, which data each agent can reach, who approves an account-level connector, and who's accountable if a client file leaks. That fence goes up around the shared space, not around any one person.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same four-fenced-nodes-plus-shared-center composition, now with a new fence drawn around the shared center too, labeled with the three rules

production_viz.label: The anchor returns - a fence drawn around the shared center
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical — four fenced nodes, shared folder center. Now a new teal fence draws itself around the shared center too. Three labels appear beside it: 'DATA SCOPE', 'CONNECTOR APPROVAL', 'ACCOUNTABILITY'.

beats.narration_text: Four careful people are not automatically a careful team. The team's safety lives in the fence around what they share — not in how carefully each person acts alone.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I'm setting up agent usage policies for a team of engineers who each use Claude responsibly on their own. Explain the team fence gap: what failure mode emerges at the team level even when every individual is careful — and give me the minimum shared-rule structure that closes it. Liam, in for Bear.
